subject: relationships
topic: Why your most reliable friends might actually be making you more lonely
angle: While sharing more breadth of information on social networks increases attraction, sharing deeper information can actually reduce it.
title: The paradox of shared intimacy

hooks.text: Are your secrets making you lonely?
You share more to connect. The evidence says it pushes people away.
You are oversharing your inner life.
A blue light illuminates an empty room.

reveal.headline: Sharing deeper information with friends can reduce attraction.
reveal.body: Increasing the depth of information in a social network profile reduces interpersonal attraction. This finding is mixed as it does not measure subjective well-being.

explain.headline: Breadth attracts. Depth repels.
explain.body: Sharing a wide range of information increases interpersonal attraction. However, increasing the depth of that information reduces it. Confidence in your character only improves when the breadth of information is low.

matters.headline: You may be pushing people away.
matters.body: That may be why sharing every intimate detail of your inner life feels isolating. You might be trading connection for exposure, creating a barrier where there should be a bridge.

example.headline: The late night scroll.
example.body: You sit in a dark room. You scroll through a friend's feed. You see their deepest secrets and feel a sudden distance instead of closeness. You put the phone down and feel alone.

stat.label: the effect of increasing depth of information in a social network profile

claims.text: Increasing the depth of information shared in a social network profile reduced interpersonal attraction.
claims.quote: Analyses indicated that, while increasing the breadth of information had a positive impact on interpersonal attraction to profile owners, increasing the depth of information reduced attraction.

claims.text: Increasing the depth of information shared in a social network profile enhanced attributional confidence only when the breadth of information shared was low.
claims.quote: Additionally, there was a significant interaction between breadth and depth of information in predicting attributional confidence; increasing the depth of information shared in an SNS profile enhanced attributional confidence only when the breadth of information shared was low.

claims.text: Increasing the breadth of information shared in a social network profile increased interpersonal attraction.
claims.quote: Analyses indicated that, higher breadth of information shared in the profile increased interpersonal attraction and that attributional confidence mediated this relationship.

claims.text: Feelings of being alone were correlated with the frequency of talking to oneself and using the TV for company.
claims.quote: Study 1 ( N = 240) found that ratings of how alone participants felt were correlated with frequency of talking to themselves and using the TV for company.

claims.text: Loneliness was correlated with talking to oneself and singing to oneself.
claims.quote: Study 2 ( N = 66) was a daily diary study where loneliness was correlated with both Study 1 behaviors and singing to oneself.

verdict: The evidence shows that social network profile depth can decrease interpersonal attraction and that loneliness is linked to behaviors that trick the brain into feeling socially interactive.
caveat: The studies on social network profiles do not measure subjective well-being or the specific impact of high-frequency, low-depth interactions with friends.
caption:
Sharing more of yourself might be making you less connected.

Research shows that while a wide breadth of information increases attraction, increasing the depth of shared information reduces it. These studies do not measure subjective well-being or the impact of low-depth interactions with friends.

How do you balance being known with being liked?
